content.title: Solving Equations with Radicals and Absolute Values
content.overview: This lesson covers solving equations that combine square roots and absolute values. Success requires managing domain restrictions from the radical and splitting the absolute value into sign-based cases to eliminate the absolute value bars before solving.
learning_objectives: Identify the domain of a radical expression by setting the radicand to be greater than or equal to zero.
Split an absolute value expression into two cases based on the sign of the inner expression.
Solve combined equations by squaring both sides and checking for extraneous solutions.

sections.title: Step 1: Establish the Radical Domain
sections.content: A square root function, √(g(x)), is only defined for real numbers when the radicand (the expression inside) is non-negative. Before solving, you must set g(x) ≥ 0. Any solution found later that does not satisfy this inequality must be discarded immediately.

sections.title: Step 2: Split the Absolute Value into Cases
sections.content: The expression |h(x)| behaves differently depending on whether h(x) is positive or negative. To solve, split the problem into two intervals: Case 1 where h(x) ≥ 0 (replace |h(x)| with h(x)) and Case 2 where h(x) < 0 (replace |h(x)| with -h(x)). This removes the absolute value bars so you can use standard algebra.

sections.title: Step 3: Square and Solve
sections.content: Once the absolute value is replaced by a standard expression, square both sides of the equation to eliminate the radical. This often results in a quadratic equation. Solve the resulting polynomial using factoring or the quadratic formula.

sections.title: Step 4: Verify and Check for Extraneous Roots
sections.content:
Squaring both sides can introduce 'extraneous solutions'—values that solve the squared equation but not the original one. You must check every candidate solution against two criteria: 1) Does it fall within the radical's domain? 2) Does it satisfy the original equation when substituted back in?

![A flowchart showing the steps: Set Domain, Split Cases, Square Both Sides, Solve, and Verify Roots.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/045539bf-76c8-4b35-833d-e8c4d7c086af-1786505857186-120.webp)

worked_examples.question: Solve for x: √(x + 3) = |x - 1|
worked_examples.solution:
1. Domain: x + 3 ≥ 0, so x ≥ -3. 
2. Split Cases: 
   Case 1 (x ≥ 1): √(x + 3) = x - 1. 
   Case 2 (-3 ≤ x < 1): √(x + 3) = -(x - 1) = 1 - x. 
3. Square both sides (same for both cases): x + 3 = (x - 1)^2 => x + 3 = x^2 - 2x + 1 => x^2 - 3x - 2 = 0. 
4. Quadratic Formula: x = [3 ± √(9 - 4(1)(-2))] / 2 = (3 ± √17) / 2. 
5. Check: (3 + √17)/2 ≈ 3.56 (fits Case 1). (3 - √17)/2 ≈ -0.56 (fits Case 2). Both are ≥ -3. Both are valid solutions.

common_mistakes: Forgetting the domain restriction: Failing to ensure the radicand is ≥ 0.
Ignoring the negative case: Only solving for |x| = x and forgetting |x| = -x.
Extraneous solutions: Accepting a root that makes the original radical equal to a negative number (which is impossible).
exam_tips: If you are short on time, plug the answer choices back into the original equation to see which ones work.
Always check if a solution makes the side with the absolute value negative; since a square root cannot equal a negative number, such solutions are invalid.
Remember that √x refers to the principal (positive) root only.
content.recap: To solve equations with radicals and absolute values, first define the domain (radicand ≥ 0), split the absolute value into two sign-based cases, square both sides to solve, and rigorously test all results in the original equation to discard extraneous roots.

knowledge_claims.content: The radicand of a square root must be greater than or equal to zero for the expression to result in a real number.
To remove absolute value bars in an equation, split the variable range into two cases: one where the inner expression is non-negative and one where it is negative.
When h(x) < 0, the expression |h(x)| is equivalent to -h(x).
Squaring both sides of an equation is the standard method to eliminate a square root radical.
Squaring both sides of an equation can introduce extraneous solutions that do not satisfy the original equation.
Every candidate solution must be checked against the radical's domain restriction (radicand ≥ 0).
A solution is only valid for a specific absolute value case if it falls within the x-interval defined for that case.
In the equation √(x + 3) = |x - 1|, the domain restriction is x ≥ -3.
The principal square root of a real number is always non-negative; therefore, the expression it equals must also be non-negative.
If squaring √(g(x)) = h(x) results in a quadratic equation, the quadratic formula can be used to find potential values for x.
The final step in solving radical-absolute value combinations is substituting candidate roots back into the original, un-squared equation.
Unlike linear equations, equations involving radicals and absolute values often yield two distinct valid solutions or no solutions at all.

videoLesson.title: Solve Radical–Absolute Equations By Cases
videoLesson.description: Recognize domain restrictions from the radicand and sign intervals from the absolute expression. Split into sign cases, square each case, then check roots against the original constraints.
